nodes.label: David Arnold
nodes.description: A historian of South Asia whose work brings medicine, science and environment into the study of colonial power. His Warwick research statement identifies these as connected fields and records his participation in the founding Subaltern Studies collective. The indexed publisher excerpt from Colonizing the Body acknowledges a debt to Foucault while refusing an uncritical application: Arnold distinguishes his emphasis on a colonial state’s production of knowledge and power. That qualified engagement is more specific than a general theoretical allegiance. His edited collections and later environmental studies extend the research programme; their complete arguments have not been read for this entry.

nodes.label: J. R. McNeill
nodes.description: An environmental historian who works across large geographical and chronological scales. nodes.label: Sheila Fitzpatrick
nodes.description: A historian of the Soviet Union whose work studies social mobility, identities and everyday practices under Stalinism. Her Sydney professional account describes how she later carried these social-history questions into the study of Stalin’s political team, examining collective practices as well as personal rule. The Russian Revolution, Stalin’s Peasants and Everyday Stalinism are selected milestones rather than a complete account of her writing on Soviet life, war and migration.

nodes.label: Patrick J. Geary
nodes.description: A medieval historian whose work links objects, social relations and historical memory. The publisher’s opening excerpt of “Sacred Commodities” treats the circulation of relics as a way to investigate the cultural conditions of exchange in a specified medieval region and period. An IAS account of Phantoms of Remembrance emphasizes that preservation and destruction of records both help shape a remembered past. It describes The Myth of Nations as challenging simple continuity between medieval identities and modern nations. These connections retain their different reading scopes; they do not make every medieval identity a modern nation or reduce sacred objects to market commodities.

nodes.label: Mike Davis
nodes.description: A historian of cities, capitalism and environmental disaster. His account of learning Marxism connects political economy, labor history and urban ecology rather than isolating theory from historical questions. In the publisher excerpt from Late Victorian Holocausts, he asks how climatic instability and systems of imperial rule combined to produce famine vulnerability; he resists attributing catastrophe to weather alone. City of Quartz and Ecology of Fear are other milestones in his investigation of Los Angeles. These selected primary passages establish an approach, while the full books and their quantitative claims remain outside this reading.

nodes.label: Hugh Trevor-Roper
nodes.description: A historian of early modern political, religious and intellectual conflicts. In his later preface to the essays first collected in 1967, he argues that England’s Puritan Revolution needs comparison with European developments and questions a simple Calvinism-to-capitalism explanation associated with Weber and Tawney. His writing on Scottish traditions also investigated the making of historical myths, though the chapter and posthumous book are not fully read here. Blair Worden’s memoir records the failed authentication of the forged Hitler diaries in 1983. That serious failure of judgment belongs alongside the scholarly programme; it is not used to erase it or to invent a causal story about his earlier abandoned projects.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Religion, the Reformation and Social Change (1967; US title The Crisis of the Seventeenth Century, 1968); “The Invention of Tradition: The Highland Tradition of Scotland” (chapter, 1983); The Invention of Scotland (posthumous, 2008).

nodes.label: Peter Gay
nodes.description: A historian of European intellectual and cultural life who used psychoanalytic questions alongside inquiry into social circumstances. His checked interview resists treating psychoanalysis as an automatic explanation that replaces historical evidence. In the publisher’s excerpt from Why the Romantics Matter, he also challenges a mechanical story of romanticism as a unified reaction against the Enlightenment, stressing divergent traditions and crosscurrents. His studies of the Enlightenment, Weimar culture and bourgeois experience mark several scales of that work. The selected interview and late excerpt do not stand for a complete reading of these multivolume studies.

nodes.description: A social and oral historian whose methodological work asks how interviews can change both historical evidence and the social purposes of historical practice. nodes.label: Kathleen Wilson
nodes.description: A historian of Britain and its eighteenth-century empire. Her first-person Stony Brook research statement describes ethnohistories of imperial culture and an inquiry into how performance helped reproduce colonial rule across Atlantic, Pacific and Indian Ocean settings. Her professional account also identifies postcolonial and feminist theory among her fields. A stated later project asks how love, violence and death enter the making of the nation-state. These are bounded research questions and methodological commitments; they do not establish agreement with every postcolonial theory or a timeless national identity.

nodes.label: Charles E. Rosenberg
nodes.description: A historian of medicine and science who treats disease as both a biological problem and a historically changing category of social experience. His primary chapter headnote asks how epidemics acquire a recognizable public form and how changing disease concepts alter social identities. It qualifies the analogy between acute outbreaks and AIDS rather than treating every epidemic as identical. The Cholera Years, The Care of Strangers and Explaining Epidemics are selected milestones in a research programme that joins institutions, disease categories and cultural responses. No contemporary clinical advice follows from these historical claims.

nodes.label: Robert Bartlett
nodes.description: A medieval historian of conquest, institutions and historical categories. In the opening of his 2001 article on race and ethnicity, he treats the terms as historically situated and politically consequential rather than neutral labels that can simply be carried across periods. This supports a contribution to the history of concepts, while leaving his complete medieval synthesis unread. Geraldine Heng later criticizes a tendency in Bartlett’s work to separate cultural distinctions from biological racism too sharply; that is her specified reading, not a verdict attributed to all medievalists. His treatment of race does not by itself establish adoption of Omi and Winant’s racial-formation theory.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Trial by Fire and Water (1986); The Making of Europe (1993); England under the Norman and Angevin Kings (2000); “Medieval and Modern Concepts of Race and Ethnicity” (2001).
nodes.scope_note: Primary 2001 article opening pp. 39–40 and selected Heng 2018 discussion of Bartlett read. Full article, books and Heng’s complete chapter unread. nodes.label: Stephen Greenblatt
nodes.description: A literary theorist associated with New Historicism. In his Harvard interview, Greenblatt connects Renaissance Self-Fashioning with colonial encounters and with questions about religion, race and sexuality, describing interpretation as an engagement between historical texts and later concerns. This contributes to cultural-historical inquiry without making literary criticism and archival history interchangeable. Sarah Maza’s 2004 discussion questions how New Historicism and historians’ cultural history meet across disciplinary boundaries; her criticism qualifies the connection. Attention to language and context alone is insufficient to place Greenblatt in the atlas’s linguistic-turn or poststructuralist programme.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Renaissance Self-Fashioning (1980); Shakespearean Negotiations (1988); Marvelous Possessions (1991).
